lesson.title: How Fast the Work Gets Done: Electrical Power
lesson.summary: Defines power as the rate at which electrical energy is transferred, derives the P = VI relationship from voltage, current, and time, and applies it to a real household appliance.
lesson.body:
Electrical energy tells you how much work gets done when charge moves through a potential difference, but it says nothing about how quickly that work happens. A car battery and a lightning bolt can both deliver similar total energy, yet one does it over minutes and the other in microseconds, and that difference matters enormously in practice. The rate at which energy is transferred or converted is called power, defined as P = W / t, where W is energy in joules and t is time in seconds. The unit of power is the watt, equal to one joule per second.

Because electrical energy already breaks down into W = QV, you can substitute that into the power definition to get P = QV / t. Current, which you already know as the rate of charge flow, is defined as I = Q / t. Rearranging the power expression to group Q and t together as Q/t reveals that P = VI: power equals voltage times current. This is one of the most used equations in all of electronics, because voltage and current are usually the two quantities you can directly measure with a meter, while energy and time are less convenient to track moment to moment.

Take a household appliance such as a hair dryer that draws 10 amps from a 120 volt outlet. Its power consumption is P = VI = 120 V times 10 A = 1200 watts, or 1.2 kilowatts. If you run that dryer for half an hour, or 0.5 hours, the energy consumed is power times time, 1.2 kW times 0.5 h = 0.6 kilowatt hours, which is the exact quantity your electric utility bills you for. Notice how the P = VI relationship and the earlier W = QV relationship are two views of the same physics, one describing rate and one describing total accumulation.

Power in a circuit is not just consumed, it is also supplied, and the same formula applies to sources. A battery delivering 2 amps at 9 volts is supplying 18 watts to whatever it is connected to. By convention, when current flows out of the positive terminal of a source into a circuit, that source is delivering power, and when current is forced backward into a source, as happens while charging a battery, that source is absorbing power instead.

Two further expressions for power become available once resistance enters the picture in the next section, P = I squared R and P = V squared divided by R, both derived by combining P = VI with Ohm's law. For now, the essential idea to carry forward is that power is always a product of an effort quantity, voltage, and a flow quantity, current, and that this product tells you the rate, in watts, at which a circuit element is converting electrical energy into some other form.

Power ratings are also how manufacturers communicate safe operating limits for real components. A resistor labeled as a quarter watt part is telling you that it can safely dissipate up to 0.25 watts as heat before it risks overheating and failing, regardless of what particular combination of voltage and current produces that dissipation. Exceed that rating, even briefly, and the excess energy has nowhere convenient to go, which is why choosing a component with an adequate power rating matters just as much as choosing the correct resistance, voltage, or current value for a given design.
